user.text: When navigating from the dashboard to a project, I want the project's title to appear instantly, but I don't want to prefetch the rest of the project page.

history.assistant:
The build passes and confirms the behavior. The output shows `Partial Prefetching enabled` and `/projects/[slug]` is now marked `◐ (Partial Prerender)` — prerendered as static HTML with dynamic server-streamed content, which is exactly the instant-title + deferred-details behavior.

## What I changed

This Next.js 16 canary uses a new prefetching model (Cache Components + Partial Prefetching). Three coordinated changes make the title appear instantly while keeping the rest of the project page out of the prefetch:

**1. `next.config.ts`** — enabled `partialPrefetching: true`. With this on, a `<Link>` prefetches only the route's **App Shell** (static + non-URL cached content) by default; URL-specific content streams in after navigation.

**2. `app/projects/[slug]/page.tsx`** — split the single `<Suspense>` into two boundaries:
- **Title** — its own `<Suspense>`, no `navigation()`. It depends on `params.slug` (URL data), so it's not in the App Shell by itself, but it gets resolved at prefetch time by the link's `prefetch={true}` (next change) and is cached (`getProjectTitle` uses `'use cache'`), so it renders with no fallback on click.
- **Details** — its own `<Suspense>` with `await navigation()` placed *above* the data access. `navigation()` excludes everything below it from **both** the App Shell and per-link prefetches, so the description + activity list are never prefetched; they stream in only after the user navigates, showing the `Loading details...` fallback meanwhile. The `'use cache'` directive stays on `getProjectDetails` (called below `navigation()`), so it keeps its cache lifetime — per the docs, `navigation()` must sit outside the cached scope.

**3. `app/page.tsx`** — added `prefetch={true}` to the dashboard `<Link>`s. This opts the link into a per-link prefetch that resolves the title's URL data before the click, which is what makes the title *instant*. Without it the title would still stream in after navigation (just fast, not instant).

## Verification
- `next build` → `✓ Compiled successfully`, TypeScript passed, `Partial Prefetching enabled`, and `/projects/[slug]` is now `◐ (Partial Prerender)`.
- The standalone `tsc` `PageProps` errors are pre-existing (the original file used the same global type, which Next generates into `.next/dev/types` during build) and unrelated to these edits.

One trade-off to note: `prefetch={true}` costs one server invocation per visible link into the route. With only two projects that's negligible; if this dashboard ever shows a large grid of project cards, consider switching to hover-triggered prefetching (the `prefetch={active ? null : false}` pattern) so you only pay for links the user is likely to click.

20 	A navigation is **instant** when the browser can start rendering the new page the moment the user clicks, with static, cached, and fallback content showing up right away, while the server streams the remaining content into its fallbacks.

4  	---
5  	
6  	Prefetching makes navigating between routes feel instant. By default, Next.js prefetches routes based on the links in your application code.
7  	
8  	This guide explains how prefetching works, what Next.js prefetches for you, and how to control it:

11 	- [What Next.js prefetches automatically](#what-nextjs-prefetches-automatically)

13 	- [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting)
14 	
15 	> **Using Partial Prefetching?** With [`partialPrefetching`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/partialPrefetching) enabled, `<Link>` defaults to prefetching a per-route [App Shell](/docs/app/glossary#app-shell) rather than the full page. See [Partial Prefetching](#partial-prefetching) below and [Adopting Partial Prefetching](/docs/app/guides/adopting-partial-prefetching) for the adoption path.
16 	
17 	## How does prefetching work?
18 	
19 	When navigating between routes, the browser requests assets for the page like HTML and JavaScript files. Prefetching is the process of fetching these resources _ahead_ of time, before you navigate to a new route.
20 	
21 	Next.js automatically splits your application into smaller JavaScript chunks based on routes. Instead of loading all the code upfront like traditional SPAs, only the code needed for the current route is loaded. This reduces the initial load time while other parts of the app are loaded in the background. By the time you click the link, the resources for the new route have already been loaded into the browser cache.
22 	
23 	When navigating to the new page, there's no full page reload or browser loading spinner. Instead, Next.js performs a [client-side transition](/docs/app/getting-started/linking-and-navigating#client-side-transitions), making the page navigation feel instant.
24 	
25 	## What Next.js prefetches automatically
26 	
27 	Next.js prefetches automatically in production. As each `<Link>` enters the viewport, Next.js prefetches the route behind it and schedules the work so a page full of links doesn't flood the network. How much of each route it prefetches depends on whether the route is static or dynamic, and changes when [Partial Prefetching](#partial-prefetching) is enabled.
28 	
29 	### Prefetching static vs. dynamic routes
30 	
31 	Without Cache Components, a static route is prefetched in full, while a dynamic route is skipped unless it has a [`loading.js`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/loading) boundary.
32 	
33 	|                                                         | **Static page** | **Dynamic page**                                                                |
34 	| ------------------------------------------------------- | --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
